1.pericope_label: And when Rehoboam was come to Jerusalem, he gathered of the house of Judah and Benjamin an hundred and fourscore thousand chosen men, which were warriors, to fight against Israel, that he might bring the kingdom again to Rehoboam. But the word of the Lord came to Shemaiah the man of God, saying, Speak unto Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all Israel in Judah and Benjamin, saying, Thus saith the Lord, Ye shall not go up, nor fight against your brethren: return every man to his house: for this thing is done of me. And they obeyed the words of the Lord, and returned from going against Jeroboam.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the opening almost entirely as a comparison with the parallel in Kings and draws a judgement out of it: the chronicler omits the verse relating the call of Jeroboam to the throne of Israel, abridges the muster, uses a different word for the kingdom and the longer form of the prophet's name, and where Kings has the house of Judah and Benjamin and the remnant of the people writes instead all Israel in Judah and Benjamin. He allows this may be a mere abbreviation but thinks there may be a hint that Judah and Benjamin were the true Israel and the apostate North had forfeited the name, while noting that others suppose a reference to northern tribesmen settled in the south and that the Syriac and Greek read the clause differently again. He holds that by the significant expression king of Judah accomplished facts receive at the outset the seal of divine assent, observes that the chronicler avoided a tautology Kings produces, and records that the rest of the chapter is wanting in the Syriac and Arabic versions, which substitute material out of Kings and then break off without finishing the prophecy of Ahijah. Delitzsch gives the sequence plainly, that Rehoboam wished to compel the ten tribes by arms and levied all the men capable of bearing arms in the two tribes until the prophet commanded him to desist.

Henry takes the four verses as a study in three characters successively assumed: Rehoboam acts first like a bold man in raising an army, with Judah and Benjamin ready to give the best assistance they could for the recovery of his right; then like a conscientious man in letting the design fall when God forbade it, either because he reverenced the divine authority or because he knew that going against the command he would not prosper but risk losing what he still had, from which Henry draws the rule that it is dangerous to undertake anything contrary to the will of God but especially a war; and last like a discreet man in seeing that it was to no purpose to think of reducing those who had revolted and fortifying his own country instead. He notices that God addresses him as the son of Solomon, taking it to intimate that the loss was determined for Solomon's sin and that it would be to no purpose to oppose a decree already gone forth, and that they obeyed although it looked mean and would turn to their reproach among their neighbours.

debates: What the chronicler means by all Israel in Judah and Benjamin, where Ellicott weighs a mere abbreviation of the fuller phrase in Kings against a hint that the two faithful tribes were the true Israel, with a third view that northern tribesmen settled in the south are meant.
Why Rehoboam abandoned the campaign, which Henry divides between reverence for the divine authority and a calculation that going against the command he would lose what he still had.
What the title king of Judah is doing at this point, which Ellicott takes as the seal of divine assent set on accomplished facts at the very outset of the account.
outliers: Henry's verdict on the lost opportunity is the sharpest thing in the passage: a few good words might have prevented the defection, but now all the forces of his kingdom cannot bring them back.

Ellicott records that the remainder of this chapter is wanting in the Syriac and Arabic versions, which substitute a run of material out of Kings and then break off abruptly without finishing the prophecy of Ahijah.
themes: And when Rehoboam was come to Jerusalem, he gathered of the house of Judah and Benjamin an hundred and fourscore thousand chosen men, which were warriors, to fight against Israel, that he might bring the kingdom again to Rehoboam.
But the word of the Lord came to Shemaiah the man of God, saying,

5.pericope_label: And Rehoboam dwelt in Jerusalem, and built cities for defence in Judah. He built even Beth–lehem, and Etam, and Tekoa, And Beth–zur, and Shoco, and Adullam, And Gath, and Mareshah, and Ziph, And Adoraim, and Lachish, and Azekah, And Zorah, and Aijalon, and Hebron, which are in Judah and in Benjamin fenced cities. And he fortified the strong holds, and put captains in them, and store of victual, and of oil and wine. And in every several city he put shields and spears, and made them exceeding strong, having Judah and Benjamin on his side.

schools.summary: Ellicott plots the list of fortified cities and reaches a conclusion that cuts against the obvious reading: all but two of the fifteen lay south and west of Jerusalem, so Rehoboam appears to have been more afraid of an attack from the south and west, that is from the Egyptians, than of a war with the northern kingdom, the two exceptions Zorah and Aijalon lying farthest north and perhaps having become Benjamite at the migration of Dan. On the places he is candid about what is unsettled, leaving Gath uncertain and proposing a candidate for Adullam. On what fortifying meant he renders the verb as strengthened, that is put into an efficient condition for defence by providing commandants and stores of arms and food, notes that the word for the strongholds and the phrase rendered made them exceeding strong are both peculiar to the chronicler, and reads the last clause as a definition of Rehoboam's territory. Delitzsch takes no view of the strategy but closes the account where the list closes, observing that the final clause answers the statement in the previous chapter that Israel had revolted and rounds off the record of all Rehoboam did to consolidate his kingdom; he says of Gath that it was a royal city of the Philistines, under Solomon the seat of its own subject king, and has not yet been certainly discovered, and of Adullam that it has not been discovered either, rejecting one conjecture as hardly correct.

Gill will not allow the Gath of this list to be the Philistine city at all, holding it a city in the tribe of Judah of which we nowhere else read, unless it is the same as the Gath compounded with another name elsewhere.

Clarke reads the same list the other way and without hesitation, holding that Rehoboam was obliged to strengthen his frontiers against the encroachments of the men of Israel and noting that Jeroboam did the same on his part to prevent inroads from Judah; on the stores he adds the point about purpose that neither of the others makes, that the provisions were laid up not only to enable the cities to endure a siege but also so that they might be able, from their situation, to supply desolate places.

debates: What Rehoboam was fortifying against, where Ellicott infers from the position of the cities that he feared Egypt more than the northern kingdom, while Clarke holds without qualification that he was strengthening his frontiers against the men of Israel.
Which Gath is meant, where Delitzsch takes it for the Philistine royal city, undiscovered, and Gill denies it can be that city at all and makes it an otherwise unrecorded town of Judah.
Where Adullam stood, which Delitzsch says has not yet been discovered while rejecting one proposed site as hardly correct, and for which Ellicott offers a different candidate again.
outliers: Clarke notes that the stores were laid up not only against a siege but so that the fortified cities might supply desolate places from their situation.
Ellicott observes that the chronicler's words for the strongholds and for making them exceeding strong are both forms of expression peculiar to him.

13.pericope_label: And the priests and the Levites that were in all Israel resorted to him out of all their coasts. For the Levites left their suburbs and their possession, and came to Judah and Jerusalem: for Jeroboam and his sons had cast them off from executing the priest’s office unto the Lord: And he ordained him priests for the high places, and for the devils, and for the calves which he had made. And after them out of all the tribes of Israel such as set their hearts to seek the Lord God of Israel came to Jerusalem, to sacrifice unto the Lord God of their fathers. So they strengthened the kingdom of Judah, and made Rehoboam the son of Solomon strong, three years: for three years they walked in the way of David and Solomon.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads Jeroboam's arrangements as deliberate policy, two centres of worship established within his own dominions so that his subjects might cease to visit the temple, and priests chosen promiscuously from all classes appointed in a direct blow at the Levitical order; such local sanctuaries existed not only at the two famous centres but in other cities of the north. He makes the chapter's sharpest claim about the calves, that since they represented the God of Israel it appears Jeroboam encouraged a system of syncretism or mixture of worships, and renders the word for devils as satyrs, literally goats, indicating a prevalence of debasing idolatry. He takes the phrase about Jeroboam's sons, with Keil, for his successors on the throne, quotes Bertheau in defence of the record's antiquity and draws from it the explanation of Jeroboam's abstention from molesting Judah, and notes drily that the countenance Solomon in his old age gave to foreign religions is here again ignored by the chronicler.

Clarke gives the political motive for the expulsion, that Jeroboam feared the priests would turn the hearts of the people to the true God and then they would revolt to Judah, and therefore established a new worship and made new gods; he supplies the reason behind the goats that Ellicott leaves out, that as the golden calves were in imitation of the Egyptian ox-god so divine honours were no doubt paid to the goat, which was an object of religious veneration in Egypt; he reckons the gains of the migration as all the truly pious out of every tribe and the whole tribe of Levi and probably part of Simeon; and he counts the years on the other side of the boundary, three of prosperity and fourteen of unfaithfulness except at such intervals as the hand of God's judgments was upon them.

Henry explains the departure of the priests and Levites most fully, holding that Jeroboam cast them off by setting up a worship they could not in conscience comply with while forbidding them to go up to Jerusalem, and was very willing they should turn themselves out to make room for the mean and scandalous persons he ordained for the high places; no marvel, he adds, if he that cast off God cast off his ministers. He gives three reasons why the Levites abandoned cities in which their maintenance had seemed well settled: they could do no good among neighbours in whom the old proneness to idolatry had revived, they would be under continual temptation to base compliances and in danger of being drawn insensibly into evil, and if they kept their integrity they had reason to expect persecution.

debates: What the worship Jeroboam established actually was, where Ellicott reads it as syncretism, since the calves represented the God of Israel, while Clarke reads the goats as straightforward Egyptian borrowing alongside the Egyptian ox-god.

Whether the record of this migration can be trusted, which Ellicott defends by quoting Bertheau that pressure from the north would antecedently produce greater earnestness in the south, and which he then uses to explain why Jeroboam left Judah alone.

What followed the three faithful years, which Clarke reckons as fourteen years of unfaithfulness broken only by intervals of judgment, while Ellicott simply refers the question forward to the next chapter.
outliers: Clarke traces the goats of this worship to Egypt, as the golden calves were traced to the Egyptian ox-god, the goat being an object of religious veneration there.
Ellicott notes that the countenance Solomon in his old age gave to foreign religions is here again ignored by the chronicler.

18.pericope_label: And Rehoboam took him Mahalath the daughter of Jerimoth the son of David to wife, and Abihail the daughter of Eliab the son of Jesse; Which bare him children; Jeush, and Shamariah, and Zaham. And after her he took Maachah the daughter of Absalom; which bare him Abijah, and Attai, and Ziza, and Shelomith. And Rehoboam loved Maachah the daughter of Absalom above all his wives and his concubines: (for he took eighteen wives, and threescore concubines; and begat twenty and eight sons, and threescore daughters.) And Rehoboam made Abijah the son of Maachah the chief, to be ruler among his brethren: for he thought to make him king. And he dealt wisely, and dispersed of all his children throughout all the countries of Judah and Benjamin, unto every fenced city: and he gave them victual in abundance. And he desired many wives.

schools.summary: Ellicott denies that Rehoboam infringed the law of the firstborn in preferring Abijah, naming the commentary that alleged it and answering that the right of the firstborn was only a double share of a man's property and not the succession, with a precedent from Solomon's accession; he would render the appointment more exactly as making Abijah head, that is prince, among his brethren. His textual work on the genealogy is the chapter's most careful: the reading daughter rather than son is right on the authority of the Greek and Latin and many Hebrew manuscripts; Jerimoth does not occur among David's sons unless the name is a corruption of Ithream, so he was probably a son of the concubines; the conjunction before Abihail is absent from the Hebrew but supplied by the Greek, and only one wife is mentioned, since a daughter of David's eldest brother could hardly become the wife of David's grandson; Maachah called the daughter of Absalom must be his granddaughter, Tamar being named elsewhere as his one daughter; and even the number of concubines is doubtful, Josephus giving thirty, the difference in Hebrew being one letter, and the recurrence of the same number in the count of daughters being suspicious.

Clarke holds that Rehoboam did break the law, since Abijah was certainly not the firstborn and was preferred because his mother was loved above the other wives, probably through her influence, this sort of preference being forbidden in Deuteronomy though he had a sort of precedent in David's preference for Solomon. He calls eighteen wives and sixty concubines bad enough but not so abandoned as his father, counts eighty-eight children, and observes that to the education of the whole Rehoboam could pay little attention since numerous families are often neglected; he grants that Rehoboam was much addicted to women while noting that we do not find he formed any heathenish alliances, makes the dispersal of the sons a defensive policy since they were unlikely to league with Jeroboam against their father, and reports the Targum's explanation that Maachah's name was changed to the more excellent Michaiah and her father's to Uriel so that the name of Absalom might not be remembered.

Henry reads the dispersal of the sons as the same policy from the other end, either that they might not be rivals to the son designed for the succession or rather because Rehoboam could repose confidence in them for preserving the public peace, trusting them with fenced cities he had taken care to victual, and he calls it after-wisdom, better than none, though dearly bought with the loss of a kingdom; he turns the comparison with Solomon into two advantages, that Rehoboam was wiser in not appearing to have married strange wives, those named here being of the family of David, and happier in having many sons and daughters where we read of only one son of Solomon's.

debates: Whether Rehoboam broke the law of the firstborn in preferring Abijah, which Clarke affirms while allowing him a precedent in David, and which Ellicott denies outright on the ground that the firstborn's right was a double share of property and not the throne.

Why the other sons were dispersed through the provinces, which Henry divides between removing rivals to the heir and trusting them with the defence of the fenced cities, while Clarke makes it purely a precaution against their leaguing with Jeroboam.

How the genealogy of these marriages should be read, where Ellicott corrects son to daughter, makes Abihail a parent rather than a second wife against the Greek and Latin, and reduces Maachah from daughter to granddaughter of Absalom.
outliers: Ellicott doubts even the number of concubines, since Josephus gives thirty, the difference in Hebrew is a single letter, and the same number recurs immediately in the count of daughters.

Clarke reports the Targum's account of why Maachah is named differently elsewhere, her name being changed to the more excellent Michaiah and her father's to Uriel so that the name of Absalom might not be remembered.
